title: A Mexican cave holds gypsum crystals 11 m long that took at least 500,000 years to grow

cover.alt: Huge white selenite crystal beams criss-crossing the Cave of the Crystals at Naica, Mexico, dwarfing the explorers in protective suits among them.

body: In April 2000, miners drilling a tunnel 300 m below Naica in Chihuahua broke into a chamber full of translucent selenite beams, a form of gypsum, the largest **11.4 m long** and an estimated 12 tonnes. A magma chamber a few kilometres down kept the groundwater there at a nearly constant temperature for an immense time: once it cooled to just below 56 °C, anhydrite in the rock slowly dissolved and gypsum, calcium sulfate with two water molecules built into each unit of its crystal, grew in its place, layer by layer, for at least 500,000 years. The cave is so hot and humid, up to 58 °C and 90 to 99% humidity, that unprotected visitors can stand it for only about ten minutes. With mining over, the pumps were switched off and the cave was allowed to reflood in October 2015.

slides.question: How hot is the air in the Cave of the Crystals?
slides.explanation: Up to 58 °C at 90 to 99% humidity. Without a cooled suit and breathing gear, a person can endure about ten minutes inside.

slides.label: the longest crystal found, about 5 m³ of selenite weighing some 12 tonnes
slides.text: Selenite is a clear, glassy form of gypsum: calcium sulfate dihydrate, CaSO4·2H2O.

steps.label: Magma 3 to 5 km down heats groundwater
Anhydrite forms in the hot water
The water cools to just below 56 °C

slides.heading: How slow is slow?
slides.text: One study measured the crystals growing at about 1.4 hundred-thousandths of a nanometre per second, which would mean the biggest took around a million years. Uranium–thorium dating puts their maximum age at about 500,000 years. Either way: at least half a million years of undisturbed, lukewarm water.

slides.question: What let the crystals grow so large?
options: A sudden flood of hot brine
slides.explanation: Groundwater heated from below stayed just under 56 °C for at least 500,000 years, so gypsum could crystallise slowly and continuously without ever dissolving again.
